q: how does a heat pump work
how does a heat pump cool a house
a: A heat pump is a device that transfers heat from one place to another using a refrigeration cycle. In summer, a heat pump cools a house by extracting heat from indoor air and releasing it outside, working like an air conditioner. In winter, it reverses the cycle, extracting heat from outdoor air (even cold air contains some heat) and transferring it indoors. Key components include: an evaporator (absorbs heat), a compressor (pressurizes refrigerant, raising its temperature), a condenser (releases heat), and an expansion valve (depressurizes refrigerant, cooling it). The refrigerant circulates through these components in a closed loop. Heat pumps are much more energy-efficient than electric resistance heaters because they move heat rather than generating it. Modern heat pumps can operate efficiently in temperatures as low as -25°C (-13°F). Types include air-source (most common), ground-source (geothermal), and mini-split (ductless) heat pumps.
